focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, like up or out. The small word is already in the sentence. Choose the verb.

tfn.s: A seller who brings in £4,000 but pays £4,500 in subscriptions, advertising and fees has made no profit.
tfn.why: The text defines profit as what remains after platform charges, subscriptions and advertising, so costs above income leave nothing.

tfn.s: The writer treats every creator who sells training as dishonest.
tfn.why: The text says: "Some experienced creators sell genuinely useful training", so the criticism is limited to some.

tfn.s: The writer implies that easy entry to digital marketplaces is both an advantage and a weakness for sellers.
tfn.why: No stock is needed, but low barriers attract competitors and products are easy to imitate.

tfn.s: The writer says commercial surveys of British side hustlers contradict the student survey.

speak.title: Role-play: should we buy the course?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You've seen an online course that costs £300 and promises money while you sleep. You want your friend to join you. Explain why it looks like a good chance and answer your friend's worries.

b.text: You're not sure the course is worth £300. Ask at least two questions about the costs, the customers and who is really making money. Suggest a cheaper way to test the idea.

phrases: I've just seen a course that teaches you to earn money online.
That's a lot of money for something we can't try first.
Who's actually making money from it?
I'd feel better if we checked the reviews together.
What would you do if it didn't work?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did you buy the course, and what made you decide?
